items.title: Choosing a degree
items.prose: A desk fits polynomials to 24 intraday spread snapshots and scores each fit on 500 fresh ones. Errors are in pence squared.
items.question: Which degree should the desk trade on?

options.text: Degree 2
Degree 10
options.why: You picked the lowest training MSE. Training error falls with every extra term, so it cannot rank models.

options.text: Degree 1
options.why: You chose the simplest model. It underfits: its test MSE of 0.32 is well above degree 2's 0.18.

options.text: Degree 6
options.why: You took the middle of the range without reading the test column. Its test MSE of 0.49 is nearly triple degree 2's.

feedback.correct: Degree 2 has the lowest test MSE, 0.18.
feedback.generic: Compare the test column, not the training one.

explain.text: Training MSE falls from 0.25 to 0.09 as the degree rises, which says nothing about new data. Test MSE bottoms at degree 2, then climbs to 2.57 at degree 10. The best fit to the training points has memorised their noise.

items.title: Impurity of a node
items.prose: A credit tree has a node holding 20 loans. Six defaulted and fourteen repaid.
items.question: What is the node's Gini impurity? Give two decimal places.

feedback.correct: The Gini impurity is $1 - 0.3^2 - 0.7^2 = 0.42$.
feedback.generic: Use $G = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2$ with the shares of defaults and repayments.

byKey.rate: You gave the default rate, 0.3. Gini is $1 - p_D^2 - p_R^2$, which is not $p_D$.
byKey.half: You computed $p(1-p) = 0.21$. With two classes the Gini is twice that, $2p(1-p)$.

explain.text: The class shares are $p_D = 0.3$ and $p_R = 0.7$, so $G = 1 - 0.09 - 0.49 = 0.42$. A pure node scores 0. An even split scores the maximum, 0.5.

items.title: Which barrier first?
items.prose: A long trade enters at £50.00. Volatility at entry is 1.5%, and the barriers sit $2\sigma$ either side. The time limit is 8 days.
items.question: What is the triple-barrier label?

options.text: −1, stopped out on day 4
+1, because the path later closes above the upper barrier
options.why: You read the whole path. Only the first barrier touched counts, and the stop came first.

options.text: 0, because the path ends only £1.80 above the entry
options.why: You used the final close. A time-out is labelled 0 only when no barrier is touched.

options.text: −1, stopped out on day 3
options.why: You treated any close below £50.00 as the stop. The stop is £48.50, first crossed on day 4.

feedback.correct: The lower barrier is touched first, on day 4.
feedback.generic: Find each barrier in pounds, then read the closes in order until one is touched.

explain.text: The barriers are $50 \times 1.03$, which is £51.50, and $50 \times 0.97$, which is £48.50. Day 4 closes at £48.40 and touches the lower one first. Later closes cannot change the label.

items.title: Staking a coin flip with odds
items.prose: A model says a trade wins with probability 0.5. A win pays £1.50 per £1 staked, and a loss costs the £1.
items.question: What fraction of capital does full Kelly stake? Give three decimal places.

feedback.correct: Kelly stakes $f = 0.5 - 0.5/1.5 = 0.167$ of capital.
feedback.generic: Use $f = p - (1-p)/b$ with $b = 1.5$.

byKey.even-odds: You used $2p - 1$, which holds only when a win pays £1 per £1. Here $b = 1.5$, so the bet has an edge.
byKey.edge: You gave the expected profit per £1, 0.25. Kelly divides that edge by the odds $b$.
byKey.half: You halved the answer. That is half Kelly, not the full Kelly fraction.

explain.text: Kelly is $f = p - (1-p)/b = 0.5 - 0.5/1.5 = 0.167$. The bet has an edge although $p = 0.5$, because a win pays more than a loss costs. At even odds the formula would give 0.

items.title: Counting fits
items.prose: A researcher tunes a ridge penalty on 800 loans. `GridSearchCV` tries 6 values of alpha with 5-fold cross-validation and the default `refit=True`.
items.question: How many times is a Ridge model fitted in total?

feedback.correct: There are $6 \times 5 = 30$ fold fits plus one refit.
feedback.generic: Count one fit for each pair of alpha and fold, then add what `refit=True` does at the end.

byKey.no-refit: You counted $6 \times 5 = 30$ and stopped. With `refit=True` the winner is fitted once more on all training rows.
byKey.values: You counted the alphas only. Each alpha is fitted once per fold.
byKey.added: You added 6 and 5. Every alpha meets every fold, so multiply.
byKey.per-fold: You counted the folds only. The search repeats them for each alpha.

explain.text: Each of the 6 values is fitted on 5 training folds, which is 30 fits. The search then refits the best alpha once on all the rows. That makes 31.

items.title: Slope past the last knot
items.prose: A desk fits a linear spline to a bond's funding spread, in basis points, against maturity $m$ in years: $\hat f(m) = 4 - m + 2(m - 3)^+ + 1.5(m - 7)^+$.
items.question: By how many basis points does the fitted spread rise for each extra year of maturity beyond 7 years?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Past a knot, every hinge before it is switched on, and the slopes add.

byKey.last-hinge: You took only the last hinge's coefficient. Beyond 7 both hinges are on, on top of the base slope $-1$.
byKey.no-base: You added the two hinges and left out the base slope, $-1$ from the $-m$ term.
byKey.base-sign: You took the base slope as $+1$. The term is $-m$, so it is $-1$.

explain.text: For $m > 7$ both hinges equal $m - 3$ and $m - 7$, so each adds its coefficient to the slope. The slope is the base $-1$ plus 2 plus 1.5, which is 2.5 bp a year. Between 3 and 7 it is $-1 + 2 = 1$.

items.title: Which model has the lower expected test error?
items.prose: Noise in next-day volume has variance 4. Three models were refitted on 200 resamples, which gave each one's bias and variance at one point. Expected test MSE is noise plus bias squared plus variance.
items.question: Fill in the expected test MSE of each model.

feedback.correct: Ridge has the lowest expected test error, 7.50.
feedback.generic: Add the noise variance 4, the squared bias and the variance.

byKey.r0c3: Square the bias first: $0.7^2 = 0.49$. Then add $4 + 0.49 + 5.51$.
byKey.r1c3: Square the bias first: $1.2^2 = 1.44$. Then add $4 + 1.44 + 2.06$.
byKey.r2c3: Square the bias first: $2.4^2 = 5.76$. Then add $4 + 5.76 + 0.34$.

explain.text: Expected test MSE is $4 + \text{bias}^2 + \text{variance}$, which gives 10.00, 7.50 and 10.10. Ridge accepts some bias to cut variance by more than the bias costs. The noise of 4 is a floor that no model can beat.

items.title: Shrunk boosting by hand
items.prose: Six trades of sizes 1 to 6 have impact $y$ in basis points: 2, 4, 3, 8, 9, 10. Round 1 fits one stump, which splits between sizes 3 and 4 and predicts the mean of each side. Boosting starts from 0 and shrinks each tree by a learning rate of 0.5.
items.question: Fill in the missing cells after round 1.

feedback.correct: The stump predicts 1.5 and 4.5 after shrinking, and the squared residuals sum to 71.5.
feedback.generic: Take each side's mean, multiply by 0.5, then subtract from $y$.

byKey.r0c2: The left mean is $(2 + 4 + 3)/3 = 3$. The learning rate scales it: $0.5 \times 3 = 1.5$.
byKey.r3c2: The right mean is $(8 + 9 + 10)/3 = 9$. The learning rate scales it: $0.5 \times 9 = 4.5$.
byKey.r3c3: A residual is $y$ minus the shrunk prediction: $8 - 4.5 = 3.5$. Using the unshrunk 9 would give $-1$.
byKey.r6c3: Square the six residuals and add: 0.25, 6.25, 2.25, 12.25, 20.25 and 30.25.

explain.text: The stump predicts 3 on the left and 9 on the right, and shrinking halves both. Each residual is $y$ minus that shrunk value. The squared residuals sum to 71.5, down from 274 with no model.

items.title: Choosing d
items.prose: A desk fractionally differences the log of a price, with weights cut off below $10^{-4}$. Its rule keeps the smallest $d$ whose variance ratio is below 0.2. That is the most memory the series can keep and still pass. The table comes from 1,500 seeded days.
items.question: Which $d$ does the rule choose?

options.why: You kept the most memory, with correlation 0.95. But its variance ratio of 0.263 fails the rule.
You rounded 0.202 down to 0.2. The ratio must be below 0.2, so $d = 0.4$ just fails.
It passes, but 0.45 also passes and keeps more memory. The rule asks for the smallest passing $d$.
You chose the plain return. It passes, but its correlation with the level is 0.04, so the memory is gone.

feedback.correct: The smallest $d$ below 0.2 is $d = 0.45$.
feedback.generic: Find the first row whose variance ratio is under 0.2.

explain.text: The ratio is 0.202 at $d = 0.4$, which fails, and 0.166 at $d = 0.45$, which passes. Larger $d$ also passes but throws memory away. The correlation with the level falls from 0.85 to 0.04 at $d = 1$.

items.title: What cost can the smoothed signal bear?
items.prose: A signal earns 3.6 basis points a day gross and trades 0.45 of capital a day. A no-trade band smooths it: turnover falls to 0.30 and gross falls to 3.3 basis points a day. Costs are charged on every unit traded.
items.question: At what one-way cost, in basis points per unit traded, does the smoothed signal break even?

feedback.correct: Break-even is $3.3/0.30 = 11$ basis points per unit.
feedback.generic: Net P&L a day is gross minus cost times turnover. Set it to zero.

byKey.unsmoothed: You used the unsmoothed numbers, $3.6/0.45 = 8$. The band changes both gross and turnover.
byKey.no-turnover: You gave the gross, 3.3. Costs fall on the units traded, so divide by the turnover of 0.30.
byKey.product: You multiplied gross by turnover. Break-even divides: the gross per day over the units traded per day.

explain.text: Net P&L per day is gross minus cost times turnover, and it is zero at $c^* = 3.3/0.30 = 11$ basis points. The unsmoothed signal breaks even at 8. Smoothing buys 3 basis points of room.

items.title: How many trees?
items.prose: A desk forecasts next-day volatility with boosted trees. The rows are in date order, and the last rows must stay unseen when the trees are fitted.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor

def early_stop_round(X, y, n_train, learning_rate):
    """Rows are in date order. Fit 300 depth-2 trees on
    the first n_train rows, score every stage on the
    rows after them, and return (best_round,
    validation_mse): the 1-based round with the lowest
    validation MSE, and that MSE rounded to 4 places."""
    model = GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=300, learning_rate=learning_rate,
                                      max_depth=2, random_state=0)
    model.fit(X[:n_train], y[:n_train])
    mse = [float(np.mean((p - y[n_train:]) ** 2)) for p in model.staged_predict(X[n_train:])]
    best = int(np.argmin(mse))
    return best + 1, round(mse[best], 4)
widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests on seeded data. The first run loads scikit-learn, which can take 20 to 40 seconds. Later runs take a second or so.
widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_vol(seed, n=400):
    """Next-day volatility of a share (% a year), days in date order.
    Five z-scored signals; two of them interact; noise sd 3."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.standard_normal((n, 5))
    y = 20 + 3 * np.tanh(2 * X[:, 0]) + 2 * X[:, 1] * X[:, 2] + 2 * X[:, 3] + rng.normal(0, 3, n)
    return X, y

feedback.correct: The trees train on the early rows and the stage curve is read on the later ones.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Fit on the first `n_train` rows only, then score every stage on the rows after them.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 fits on the first 250 days and scores the last 150. A shuffled split or a training score gives a different round.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 expects the round counted from 1. `argmin` counts from 0.
byKey.error: If the starter stopped, fill in the function body first. Python reports the line.

explain.text: `staged_predict` gives the forecast after each tree, so one fit yields the whole validation curve. The best round is the position of the lowest value plus one, because rounds count from 1. The validation rows come after the training rows, so the choice never uses the future.

items.title: Hidden look-ahead in a feature script
items.prose: A feature script builds a panel of daily features, one row per stock and date. Each feature at date $t$ may use only data up to the close of $t$.

params.title: features.py
lines: # eps is published 6 weeks after quarter_end

items.question: Tap every line that lets a feature see data after its date.

feedback.correct: Four lines look ahead.
feedback.generic: Check each window, each ranking group and each statistic: which dates does it read?

byKey.no-merge: You found three. The merge on `quarter_end` also looks ahead, because earnings come out weeks after that date.
byKey.l2: `pct_change(5)` looks back five days, which is allowed.
byKey.l4: Ranking within one date compares shares on that day only.
byKey.l7: A trailing 20-day window ends on the current day.
byKey.l8: `shift(1)` brings in yesterday's close, a lag.
byKey.l1: This line only groups the rows.

explain.text: A centred window reads two days past the date. Ranking by stock compares each day with that stock's whole history. The full-sample mean and sd read every date, and the merge attaches earnings weeks before they were published.

items.title: A lasso on raw units
items.prose: A desk fits a lasso for next-month return on raw features. Momentum and volatility are in %, and value is a ratio. Size is in £ millions, with sd about 7,400. Turnover is a fraction, with sd about 0.004.
items.question: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Size has a tiny coefficient per £1m, so the lasso charges it almost nothing for staying in.
Turnover needs a very large coefficient, so the lasso is likely to cut it even if it matters.
Quoting size in £ billions instead would leave the lasso fit unchanged.
options.why: You assumed units do not matter. A £1bn unit makes the coefficient 1,000 times bigger, and so its penalty.

options.text: Standardising each column with the training rows' mean and sd puts the penalty on a common scale.
Fitting the scaler on all rows is harmless, because a scaler has no coefficients.
options.why: You overlooked that its means and sds come from the rows. Test rows then shape the inputs.

options.text: Rescaling a column changes the forecasts of ordinary least squares as much as the lasso's.
options.why: You applied the penalty argument to least squares. Without a penalty, its forecasts do not change when a column is rescaled.

feedback.correct: The penalty depends on units, and training-only standardising fixes that.
feedback.generic: Ask what each unit does to the size of a coefficient, and what the lasso charges for size.

explain.text: A penalty on coefficient size depends on each feature's units. Size is huge, so its coefficient is tiny and nearly free. Turnover is tiny, so it needs a huge coefficient and gets cut.

items.title: Reading feature importance
items.prose: A random forest predicts 20-day returns for 400 shares. Its feature list includes `ticker_id`, a unique number for each share.
items.question: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Impurity importance can rank `ticker_id` high, because trees can split on a unique number to memorise rows.
Permutation importance on the training rows is a fair guide to what predicts new data.
options.why: You permuted rows the trees have memorised. Use a held-out block to see what carries over.

options.text: Permutation importance on a held-out block is near zero, or below, for a useless feature.
Two near-copies of a signal share the credit, so each looks weaker than the pair together.
A feature with zero importance has no relationship with the target.
options.why: You read zero as no link. If a near-copy is in the model, permuting one feature costs little.

options.text: Impurity importance is computed on the test set.
options.why: You swapped the methods. Impurity importance comes from the training splits; permutation importance uses rows you choose.

feedback.correct: Impurity importance can reward memorising, and held-out permutation exposes it.
feedback.generic: Ask which rows each method reads, and what happens when two features carry the same information.

explain.text: Impurity importance counts splits on the training rows, so a unique id can look useful. Permutation on held-out rows scores a useless feature near zero. Near-copies share the credit, so a low score does not prove no link.

items.title: When the effect depends on another feature
items.prose: A linear model forecasts next-month return from z-scored features: $\hat y = 0.2 + 0.5\,\text{mom} - 0.3\,\text{vol} + 0.6\,\text{mom}\times\text{vol}$. A share has $\text{vol} = 1.5$.
items.question: By how much does the forecast change when its momentum rises by one sd?

feedback.correct: The slope on momentum is $0.5 + 0.6 \times 1.5 = 1.4$.
feedback.generic: Hold vol fixed and collect every term that contains mom.

byKey.main: You used the main effect only. The interaction adds $0.6 \times \text{vol}$ to momentum's slope.
byKey.product: You gave the interaction part alone, $0.6 \times 1.5$. The main effect of 0.5 still applies.
byKey.added: You added 0.5 and 0.6 without using vol. The interaction coefficient multiplies vol.

explain.text: With vol fixed, momentum's slope is $0.5 + 0.6\,\text{vol}$. At vol = 1.5 that is $0.5 + 0.9 = 1.4$. The interaction makes momentum matter more when volatility is high.

items.title: Variance of a forest
items.prose: Each tree's prediction for one loan has variance $\sigma^2 = 9$. Any two trees' predictions have correlation $\rho = 0.25$. A forest averages $B = 200$ trees.
items.question: What is the variance of the forest's prediction? Give two decimal places.

feedback.correct: The variance is $\rho\sigma^2 + (1-\rho)\sigma^2/B = 2.28$.
feedback.generic: Use $\text{Var} = \rho\sigma^2 + (1-\rho)\sigma^2/B$ for an average of correlated predictions.

byKey.independent: You divided $\sigma^2$ by $B$, as for independent trees. Correlated trees keep the part $\rho\sigma^2$.
byKey.floor: You gave $\rho\sigma^2$ alone. The second term, $(1-\rho)\sigma^2/B = 0.034$, is small but not zero.
byKey.one-tree: That is one tree's variance. Averaging 200 trees must lower it.
byKey.mixed: You gave $(1-\rho)\sigma^2$. Dividing it by $B$ is what averaging does.

explain.text: The average of correlated predictions has variance $\rho\sigma^2 + (1-\rho)\sigma^2/B$. Here that is $2.25 + 0.034 = 2.28$. More trees shrink only the second term, which is why random forests decorrelate their trees.

items.title: A crash detector that is mostly right
items.prose: A classifier flags crash days over 1,000 trading days. It raised 40 alarms and caught 10 of the 25 crashes.
items.question: Fill in the four measures as decimals.

rows: Accuracy of always saying no crash

feedback.correct: Precision 0.25, recall 0.40, and accuracy of 0.955 against 0.975 for never alarming.
feedback.generic: Read the counts: 10 caught, 30 false alarms, 15 missed, 945 quiet days called right.

byKey.r0c1: Precision is the share of alarms that were real: 10 of 40.
byKey.r1c1: Recall is the share of crashes caught: 10 of 25.
byKey.r2c1: Accuracy counts both kinds of right call: $(10 + 945)/1000$.
byKey.r3c1: Never alarming is right on all 975 quiet days.

explain.text: Precision is 10/40 = 0.25 and recall is 10/25 = 0.40. Accuracy is 955/1,000, yet saying no crash every day scores 975/1,000. For rare events, accuracy hides a poor detector.

items.title: Inside the street
items.prose: A linear support vector classifier has $w = (2, -1)$ and $b = 1$, scaled so that the edges of its street are $w \cdot x + b = 1$ and $w \cdot x + b = -1$. New points arrive with two standardised features $(x_1, x_2)$.
items.question: Which points lie strictly inside the street? Select all that apply.

options.why: Its decision value is $2 + 1 = 3$, beyond the $+1$ edge. A large value is a confident call, not a point in the street.
Its value is $-2.5 + 1 = -1.5$, beyond the $-1$ edge. A negative value is the other class, not the street.
Its value is exactly $b = 1$, so it sits on the edge, where a support vector would. Strictly inside needs a value between $-1$ and 1.

feedback.correct: Their decision values are 0.5, $-0.5$ and 0.4, all between $-1$ and 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $2x_1 - x_2 + 1$ for each point; inside the street means a value strictly between $-1$ and 1.

explain.text: The street is where $-1 < w \cdot x + b < 1$. The values are 0.5 for $(0.2, 0.9)$, $-0.5$ for $(-0.5, 0.5)$ and 0.4 for $(-1, -1.4)$, so those three are inside. The others give 3, $-1.5$ and exactly 1, the last on the edge.

items.title: Two groups of spreads
items.prose: Seven bonds' bid-ask spreads, in basis points: 2, 3, 7, 11, 12, 13 and 22. Run k-means with two centres, starting at 2 and 3, until no bond changes group.
items.question: What is the inertia where it stops?

feedback.correct: It stops with groups 2, 3, 7 and 11, 12, 13, 22, centres 4 and 14.5, and inertia $14 + 77 = 91$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Assign each bond to the nearer centre, then move each centre to its group's mean. Repeat until no bond moves.

byKey.early-stop: You stopped at centres 2.5 and 13. The bond at 7 is then nearer 2.5 than 13, so it moves and the centres move again.
byKey.unsquared: You added the plain distances to the final centres. Inertia adds the squared distances.

explain.text: From 2 and 3 the centres move to 2 and 11.33, then 2.5 and 13, then 4 and 14.5. There no bond moves, and the groups are 2, 3, 7 and 11, 12, 13, 22. The inertia is $(4 + 1 + 9) + (12.25 + 6.25 + 2.25 + 56.25) = 14 + 77 = 91$.

items.title: One weight's slope
items.prose: A one-unit network scores a trade from two features: $h = \max(0,\ w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b)$ and $\hat y = v h$, with loss $L = \tfrac12(\hat y - y)^2$. For one trade $x = (1, 3)$ and $y = 1$, with $w_1 = 0.5$, $w_2 = -0.2$, $b = 0.4$ and $v = 2$.
items.question: What is $\partial L / \partial w_2$ at these weights?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Chain the slopes: $L$ through $\hat y$, $\hat y$ through $h$, and $h$ through $w_2$, where the unit is on.

byKey.used-x1: You multiplied by $x_1 = 1$. The weight $w_2$ multiplies $x_2 = 3$.
byKey.slope-v: You found $\partial L / \partial v = (\hat y - y)h$. The question asks about $w_2$, one layer further back.
byKey.sign: You took $y - \hat y$. The slope of $\tfrac12(\hat y - y)^2$ in $\hat y$ is $\hat y - y = -0.4$.
byKey.no-half: You dropped the $\tfrac12$: the slope of $\tfrac12 u^2$ is $u$, not $2u$.

explain.text: The unit's input is $0.5 - 0.6 + 0.4 = 0.3 > 0$, so it is on, $h = 0.3$ and $\hat y = 0.6$. Then $\tfrac{\partial L}{\partial w_2} = (\hat y - y) \cdot v \cdot x_2 = (-0.4)(2)(3) = -2.4$. A step against it raises $w_2$, which lifts $\hat y$ towards 1.

items.title: Reading a logistic coefficient
items.prose: A logistic model for loan default has a coefficient of 0.45 on leverage, in log-odds per turn of leverage. A loan at leverage 2 has a default probability of 10%. Nothing else changes.
items.question: What is the default probability at leverage 4? Give a percentage to one decimal place.

feedback.correct: The odds rise from 0.111 to 0.273, a probability of 21.5%.
feedback.generic: The coefficient acts on the log-odds, so two more turns multiply the odds by $e^{0.9}$.

byKey.prob-times: You multiplied the probability by $e^{0.9}$. The coefficient multiplies the odds, not the probability.
byKey.odds-as-prob: You stopped at the odds, 0.273. Convert them: probability is odds over one plus odds.

explain.text: At leverage 2 the odds are $0.10/0.90 = 0.111$. Two more turns multiply them by $e^{0.45 \times 2} = 2.46$, which gives 0.273. The probability is $0.273/1.273 = 21.5\%$.

items.title: An interaction, scaled and shrunk
items.prose: A desk thinks momentum pays more when volatility is high. It adds their product as a feature and regularises with ridge. The rows are share-months in date order.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

def ridge_interaction_test_mse(X, y, alpha, n_train):
    """Rows are in date order. Train on the first n_train
    rows, test on the rest. Add one column: the
    product of the first two RAW columns. Standardise
    every column with the training rows' mean and sd
    (population sd; a constant column keeps divisor
    1). Fit Ridge(alpha=alpha) and return the test MSE
    rounded to 4 places."""
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    X = np.column_stack([X, X[:, 0] * X[:, 1]])
    mu = X[:n_train].mean(axis=0)
    sd = X[:n_train].std(axis=0)
    sd = np.where(sd == 0, 1.0, sd)
    Z = (X - mu) / sd
    model = Ridge(alpha=alpha).fit(Z[:n_train], y[:n_train])
    err = model.predict(Z[n_train:]) - y[n_train:]
    return round(float(np.mean(err ** 2)), 4)

X, y = make_months(4)
X = X.copy(); X[:, 2] = 0.6

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_months(seed, n=300):
    """Share-months in date order. Columns: momentum (%), volatility (%), value (book-to-price).
    y: next-month return in %. Momentum pays more when volatility is high."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    mom = 8.0 * rng.standard_normal(n)
    vol = 30 + 10 * rng.standard_normal(n)
    value = 0.6 + 0.3 * rng.standard_normal(n)
    y = (0.5 + 0.06 * mom - 0.02 * (vol - 30) + 0.8 * (value - 0.6)
         + 0.005 * mom * (vol - 30) + 1.0 * rng.standard_normal(n))
    return np.column_stack([mom, vol, value]), y

widget.solution:
import math

def meta_labels_trade(prices, vol, sides, pt, sl, h):
    """One meta-label per entry day t = 0 .. len(prices)
    - h - 1, skipping days where vol[t] is nan.
    sides[t] is +1 (long) or -1 (short). Profit target
    pt * vol[t] and stop sl * vol[t], both measured
    from the entry close prices[t]. A long profits
    above, a short below. Read the next h closes in
    order. Return 1 if the profit target is touched
    first; 0 if the stop is touched first or neither
    is."""
    out = []
    for t in range(len(prices) - h):
        if math.isnan(vol[t]):
            continue
        s = sides[t]
        up = prices[t] * (1 + (pt if s == 1 else sl) * vol[t])
        down = prices[t] * (1 - (sl if s == 1 else pt) * vol[t])
        label = 0
        for d in range(1, h + 1):
            p = prices[t + d]
            profit = p >= up if s == 1 else p <= down
            stop = p <= down if s == 1 else p >= up
            if stop:
                break
            if profit:
                label = 1
                break
        out.append(label)
    return out

widget.prelude:
import math
import numpy as np

def make_prices(n=750, seed=21, mu=0.0003, sigma=0.012):
    """n + 1 daily closes from 100: daily log returns mu + sigma * noise."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    r = mu + sigma * rng.standard_normal(n)
    return np.round(100 * np.exp(np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(r)])), 4).tolist()

def rolling_vol(prices, window=20):
    """vol[t]: sample sd of the last `window` simple returns ending on day t (nan before)."""
    p = np.asarray(prices, dtype=float)
    r = p[1:] / p[:-1] - 1
    vol = [float('nan')] * len(p)
    for t in range(window, len(p)):
        vol[t] = float(np.std(r[t - window:t], ddof=1))
    return vol

items.title: An honest boosted-tree study
items.prose: A researcher builds a boosted-tree model of 10-day returns from daily data. The study must use time-ordered validation from the first step.

items.title: Walk-forward folds with a purge and a window
items.prose: A desk walks forward over daily rows with a label that looks $h$ days ahead. It wants a rolling training window and a purge of the labels that reach into each test block.
items.question: Complete `walk_forward_folds(n, n_splits, test_size, h, window=None)`.

def walk_forward_folds(n, n_splits, test_size, h, window=None):
    """Walk-forward folds for a label that looks h days
    ahead (row t is labelled with days t + 1 to t +
    h). The last n_splits * test_size rows are the
    test blocks, in order, each test_size rows long. A
    fold trains on the rows before its block, minus
    the h - 1 rows whose labels reach into it; with
    window given, only the latest `window` of those
    rows. Return a list of (train_start, train_end,
    test_start, test_end), half-open ranges. Raise
    ValueError if any fold would have no training
    rows."""
    ...
widget.solution:
def walk_forward_folds(n, n_splits, test_size, h, window=None):
    """Walk-forward folds for a label that looks h days
    ahead (row t is labelled with days t + 1 to t +
    h). The last n_splits * test_size rows are the
    test blocks, in order, each test_size rows long. A
    fold trains on the rows before its block, minus
    the h - 1 rows whose labels reach into it; with
    window given, only the latest `window` of those
    rows. Return a list of (train_start, train_end,
    test_start, test_end), half-open ranges. Raise
    ValueError if any fold would have no training
    rows."""
    folds = []
    for start in range(n - n_splits * test_size, n, test_size):
        train_end = start - (h - 1)
        if train_end <= 0:
            raise ValueError("a fold has no training rows")
        train_start = 0 if window is None else max(0, train_end - window)
        folds.append((train_start, train_end, start, start + test_size))
    return folds

items.title: Betting a miscalibrated edge
items.prose: A model says a trade wins with probability 0.58 at even odds, so the desk stakes full Kelly. A calibration check later shows such trades win only 52% of the time. Growth per bet is $g(f) = p\ln(1+f) + (1-p)\ln(1-f)$.
items.question: What is the true expected log growth per bet, as a percentage, at $p = 0.52$? Give two decimal places.

widget.placeholder: a percentage, negative if it shrinks
widget.label: Growth per bet

feedback.correct: Growth is $-0.65\%$ a bet: the stake is four times the true Kelly.
feedback.generic: Full Kelly at even odds is $2p - 1$ for the model's $p$. Then score that stake with the true $p$.

byKey.believed: You scored the stake with the model's own 0.58, which gives +1.29%. The true chance is 0.52.
byKey.right-stake: That is the growth from staking 0.04, the true Kelly. The desk staked 0.16.
byKey.sign: You lost the sign. $0.52\ln 1.16 + 0.48\ln 0.84$ is negative.

explain.text: Full Kelly for the model's $p = 0.58$ is $2p - 1 = 0.16$. At the true $p = 0.52$, growth is $0.52\ln 1.16 + 0.48\ln 0.84 = -0.0065$. The true Kelly stake is 0.04, so the desk bets four times it, and an edge becomes a loss.

    2. Tune C on the training rows only: a scaler then

       accuracy over TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=4). Ties
       keep the earlier C in Cs.
    3. Refit the best pipeline on all training rows.
    4. Return (best_C, test_hit_rate, base_rate), each

       test rows whose y equals the training rows'

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit, cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

def honest_report(X, y, Cs):
    """Rows are in date order; y is 0 or 1.
    1. Test = the last 30% of rows (train = the first
       int(0.7 * n)).
    2. Tune C on the training rows only: a scaler then
       LogisticRegression(C=C), scored by mean
       accuracy over TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=4). Ties
       keep the earlier C in Cs.
    3. Refit the best pipeline on all training rows.
    4. Return (best_C, test_hit_rate, base_rate), each
       rounded to 4 places. base_rate is the share of
       test rows whose y equals the training rows'
       majority class (1 if the training mean >= 0.5)."""
    n_train = int(len(y) * 0.7)
    X_tr, X_te = X[:n_train], X[n_train:]
    y_tr, y_te = y[:n_train], y[n_train:]

    def make(C):
        return Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("clf", LogisticRegression(C=C))])

    best_C, best = None, -1.0
    for C in Cs:
        score = cross_val_score(make(C), X_tr, y_tr, cv=TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=4),
                                scoring="accuracy").mean()
        if score > best:
            best_C, best = C, score
    model = make(best_C).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    hit = float((model.predict(X_te) == y_te).mean())
    majority = 1 if y_tr.mean() >= 0.5 else 0
    base = float((y_te == majority).mean())
    return best_C, round(hit, 4), round(base, 4)

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_days(seed, n=900):
    """Daily index returns with a little mean reversion; volatility doubles after 60% of the sample.
    X: yesterday's return, the 5-day and 20-day returns, and 20-day volatility, all in %,
    known at the close of day t. y: 1 if day t + 1 closes up. Rows are in date order."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    N = n + 21
    sig = np.where(np.arange(N) < int(0.6 * N), 0.008, 0.016)
    r = np.zeros(N)
    for t in range(1, N):
        r[t] = 0.0004 - 0.25 * r[t - 1] + sig[t] * rng.standard_normal()
    c = np.cumsum(r)
    rows, ys = [], []
    for t in range(20, N - 1):
        rows.append([100 * r[t], 100 * (c[t] - c[t - 5]), 100 * (c[t] - c[t - 20]),
                     100 * np.std(r[t - 19:t + 1], ddof=1)])
        ys.append(1 if r[t + 1] > 0 else 0)
    return np.array(rows), np.array(ys)

CS = [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0]

items.title: Explaining a model note
items.prompt:
A new analyst sends this note. The model predicts next-month returns for 500 shares from 60 features, on 2010 to 2024 data.

*I standardised every feature on the full sample. Then I split the rows at random: 70% to train and 30% to test. A boosted model of 2,000 deep trees scored an R-squared of 0.45 on the training rows. On the test rows it scored 0.02. I tried 40 settings of the learning rate and the depth. The best test R-squared was 0.09, so the model works. Next I will add more features.*

Write a short reply that covers four things.

(a) Explain the gap between 0.45 and 0.02 using bias and variance. Say what regularisation would do about it.

(b) Name two leaks in the pipeline and say how each flatters the score.

(c) Say what the 0.09 is worth.

(d) Describe the validation you would use instead, in order.
items.model:
**(a) Bias and variance.** Deep trees on 60 features have low bias and high variance. They fit noise as well as signal. So the training R-squared of 0.45 measures how well they memorised the rows. The test R-squared of 0.02 shows what carries over to new months, and that is almost nothing. Adding features adds flexibility and so adds variance.

Regularisation accepts a little more bias for much less variance. For trees that means shallower trees, a smaller learning rate, bigger leaves or early stopping. For a linear model it would be a ridge or lasso penalty. The strength is chosen on validation data, never on the test rows.

**(b) Two leaks.**

- *Scaling on the full sample.* The means and sds include the test months, so the test period shapes the inputs. Fit the scaler inside each training fold, for example in a pipeline.
- *A random split of time-ordered data.* Neighbouring months overlap, so training rows next to a test month carry its answer. The model also trains on months after the ones it is tested on. Both flatter the score.

The test rows were also used to choose among 40 settings. That is a third leak: the test set was no longer unseen.

**(c) What 0.09 is worth.** It is the best of 40 tries on the same rows, so selection inflates it. Even noise would give the best of 40 a positive score. The 0.09 is an upper bound, not an estimate, and the honest figure is probably near the 0.02.

**(d) Validation in order.**

1. Hold out the last block of months as the test period. Purge the labels that reach into it.
2. Build the scaler and the model inside a pipeline.
3. Tune depth and learning rate with walk-forward folds on the earlier block. Use a gap for the label horizon, and stop the trees early.
4. Refit the chosen model on the whole earlier block.
5. Score the test block once. Report it against a simple baseline, net of costs, with the number of settings tried.

rubric.text: Reads the gap as overfitting: low bias and high variance from deep trees and many features. Training R-squared then measures memorised noise.
Says regularisation trades a little bias for much less variance. Gives an example, and tunes it on validation data.
Names two leaks, such as full-sample scaling and a random split of time-ordered data. Says how each flatters the score.
Says 0.09 is the best of 40 tries on the test rows. It is inflated by selection, so it is not an honest estimate.
Gives a time-ordered plan: test block last, purge or gap, scaler inside the pipeline. Tunes walk-forward on the earlier block, then scores the test block once.
Asks for a baseline or base rate, costs and the number of trials beside the final score.

explain.text: A large gap between training and test scores is variance, and regularisation is the cure. The leaks make the test score look better than the truth. An honest study keeps the test block last and scores it once.
